problems.description: update_task now has a polymorphic return type `dict | None | tuple`; routing errors through a stringly-typed `("invalid_status", status)` tuple forces callers (edit_task) to do fragile `isinstance(task, tuple) and task[0] == "invalid_status"` checks. A custom exception or typed result object would be cleaner and preserve the function's contract.

test_list_multiple_tasks_ordered_by_created_at_desc creates three tasks back-to-back with no delay despite the comment claiming 'slight delays'; the ordering assertion is flaky if created_at has coarse (second) precision.
Valid statuses are hardcoded as magic values in is_valid_status ("pending", "done") rather than a shared constant; a schema change would require hunting for all occurrences.

Measured convention score is 0.69 with 11 violations, but all listed offenders (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py, __init__.py) are files untouched by this commit; the diff's own additions (snake_case functions, PascalCase test classes) are compliant. The measurement reflects pre-existing debt, not this change.

strengths: Adds a comprehensive 337-line test suite covering create/list/get/update success and failure paths with correct status-code assertions (201/400/404/422).
Validation is fail-fast: status is checked before the DB write, avoiding partial/invalid updates.
Correct HTTP semantics: 422 for invalid status, 404 for missing task, and clean extraction of is_valid_status as a testable helper.
Respects surrounding module style (thin Flask routes delegating to helper functions returning dicts).
commit_reviews.summary: Adds real value (status validation + a full test suite) but ships a polymorphic tuple-based error channel in update_task that is a genuine maintainability regression, balanced against the pre-existing convention debt that this commit neither worsens nor fixes.

problems.description: Breaking API change: all /tasks endpoints now require a Bearer JWT, so every pre-existing client is rejected with 401 with no versioning, migration note, or back-compat path.

update_task's UPDATE statement filters only by id, not owner_id; ownership is enforced by a separate read (check-then-act) rather than being scoped in the write, so the guarantee is non-atomic and weaker than the other task queries.
The diff adds a large untested security surface (register/login/JWT/401 paths) with no new tests, leaving hashing, token expiry, and authorization edge cases unverified.
SECRET_KEY falls back to the well-known 'dev-secret-key-change-in-production' value; forgetting to set the env var in production yields forgeable tokens.
tasks.owner_id defaults to 1 via FK to an initially-empty users table, creating dangling references and a silent single-user assumption that SQLite will not enforce without PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON.

Token is parsed twice per request (require_auth decorator then get_current_user() again in each route body); verify_jwt_token's except tuple is redundant since ExpiredSignatureError subclasses InvalidTokenError; datetime.utcnow() is deprecated in 3.12+.
The +2 classes added in app.py are not PascalCase (measured), directly contributing to the 0.69 convention score.

strengths: Passwords are hashed with werkzeug (never stored or returned in plaintext) and task queries are scoped by owner_id end-to-end for reads.
Follows the file's existing structure: get_db() context manager, model/route separation, jsonify responses, snake_case functions.
Migration-friendly: CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS plus owner_id DEFAULT 1 lets existing rows survive without a destructive data migration.
Clear, distinct HTTP semantics (400/401/409/201) with explicit validation_error vs conflict_error handling.
commit_reviews.summary: The auth/multi-tenancy addition follows the file's internal patterns and does its security basics right, but it breaks the existing API contract, scopes the critical UPDATE without owner_id, ships untested auth logic, and — noting a discrepancy — most of the 11 measured convention violations (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, repositories.py, __init__.py) live outside this +1-file diff, so app.py itself is cleaner than the 0.69 aggregate implies.

problems.description: No DB migration for the new `email` column: `CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS` won't alter existing databases, yet only `authenticate_user` guards the missing column (via IndexError); `get_user_email` runs a bare `SELECT email FROM users` that would raise OperationalError and 500 on a legacy DB when a task is marked done.
Silent failure on import: `except Exception: pass` around the celery import swallows real import errors and disables notifications with no log or signal, making the feature's absence invisible.

New Celery/Redis dependencies are used but not declared in requirements (diff touches only app.py, celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, tests/test_app.py); the app cannot run or be tested in a fresh environment without undeclared packages.

New module constants (broker_url, result_backend, task_serializer, etc.) use snake_case while the existing app.py uses UPPER_CASE (DATABASE, SECRET_KEY), matching the measured convention violations (score 0.69; 11 violations across the new files).

Notification side-effect is embedded in the model-layer update_task rather than the route, coupling data mutation to async effects; fire-and-forget `send_task` offers no retry, ack, or observability if the broker is down.
Tests patch app.send_task_notification_email, so the actual Celery task and its config are never exercised; the queue round-trip and the notifications-queue routing remain untested.
No Celery worker for the `notifications` queue is provisioned in the story; messages will accumulate in Redis until a worker is started.

strengths: Feature is scoped and cleanly decomposed into dedicated modules (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py) instead of bloating app.py
Async email via Celery keeps the request path fast and decoupled from SMTP, with JSON serialization explicitly configured
Graceful degradation on registration: email is optional and defaults to None without breaking existing flows
Deterministic tests: mocked notification send keeps the suite runnable without a live broker/email service, and the status-transition (pending->done) trigger is explicitly covered
commit_reviews.summary: Session 3 adds a reasonable Celery-based notification subsystem with solid test coverage, but the fragile legacy-DB handling, silent exception swallowing, and undeclared dependencies introduce meaningful technical debt that tempers an otherwise neutral change.

problems.description: BaseRepository._get_db_path() defers `import app` to read app.DATABASE, creating hidden app→repo→app coupling and a circular-import workaround; configuration should be injected or read from a single config source.

Abstract contract violated: BaseRepository declares find_by_id(id) and create(**kwargs), but TaskRepository implements find_by_id(task_id, owner_id) and UserRepository.create(username, password_hash, email) — breaks Liskov substitution and weakens the abstraction the base class promises.

app.py retains get_db() even though all model queries moved to repositories; two parallel connection paths (get_db vs _get_db) now coexist, which likely drives the +3 cognitive complexity and +2 SonarQube smells.

repositories.py flagged for module-level constant casing (UPPER_CASE expected) per measurement; note the 0.69 convention score is dragged down mostly by pre-existing violations in celery_config.py/celery_tasks.py/__init__.py that this commit does not touch.

UserRepository.create returns a dict | (error, message) union, muddying the -> dict contract declared on the abstract create; inherited from the existing tuple-error convention but now formalized in a typed signature.

strengths: Data access cleanly extracted into a repository layer, removing ~90 lines of inline SQL from app.py route/model code
Abstract BaseRepository standardizes the repository contract and keeps the sqlite3.Row factory consistent
Duplication reduced (-0.4% per SonarQube) and the IndexError email fallback replaced with a safe user.get("email")
Respects existing patterns: snake_case naming, context-managed connections, and the established (error, message) tuple convention
commit_reviews.summary: A sound, net-positive repository-pattern refactor that improves layering and cuts duplication, but introduces hidden app-module coupling and abstract-method contract drift — and the 0.69 convention score mostly reflects pre-existing violations in files untouched by this commit.

problems.description: Rate limiting is silently disabled with no logging when Redis is unavailable (limiter=None), so a security control degrades to no-op without any signal.

The '100 per minute' limit is hardcoded in two places (default_limits and the per-route limiter.limit), and applying default_limits plus the per-route decorator double-applies the same limit redundantly.
The /tasks GET response contract changes from a bare JSON list to an envelope {data, next_cursor, total} — a breaking API change; tests were updated but no compatibility note or versioning was added.
A full COUNT(*) scan runs on every paginated request (including later pages) regardless of limit, which is O(n) on large task tables.
Redis host/port/db are hardcoded ('redis://localhost:6379/0') rather than read from env, inconsistent with DATABASE/SECRET_KEY which use os.environ.get.

Measured convention score is 0.69 with 11 flagged violations (PascalCase/snake_case/UPPER_CASE), though the majority sit in files outside this diff (celery_config.py, celery_tasks.py, __init__.py) and are pre-existing rather than introduced here.
Cognitive complexity +27 and +2 new smells per SonarQube, concentrated in the rate-limiter setup and pagination query branching.

strengths: Cursor-based pagination lives in the repository layer (find_paginated_by_owner), following the existing repo/route separation pattern, with a total count and next_cursor envelope.
Rate-limit keying is per-user when authenticated and falls back to IP for register/login, which is the right design for auth endpoints.
Rate limiting is cleanly disabled under TESTING so tests stay deterministic.
Defensive parsing and clamping of the limit query param (1..100).
Tests updated to match the new response envelope and cover pagination ordering.
commit_reviews.summary: A solid cross-cutting improvement (rate limiting + cursor pagination) that fits the existing layered architecture and updates tests accordingly, but carries real technical debt via a silent no-op security fallback, duplicated/redundant limit configuration, and a hardcoded Redis dependency — while the low 0.69 convention score reflects mostly pre-existing violations in untouched files rather than this diff's own (idiomatic) additions.

compounding_issues: Session 2's JWT secret defaults to a short development key (28-byte HMAC key, below RFC 7518's 32-byte minimum — surfaces as a persistent InsecureKeyLengthWarning through session 5), and security hardening was never revisited.

Session 2's ownership migration assigned pre-existing tasks to a synthetic 'legacy' user with an unguessable password; every later session inherits this awkward compatibility account rather than a clean migration.
Session 1 moved init_db() to module import time for testability, which couples database initialization to import and leaves no app-startup/CLI seam for later sessions to reuse.

Session 5's cursor pagination orders by id DESC while sessions 1-3 established created_at DESC 'newest first' ordering — a subtle ordering-semantics inconsistency between the original list endpoint and the paginated replacement.

Sessions 3 and 5 add external infrastructure (Celery/Redis broker, Flask-Limiter with Redis storage) that the test suite exercises only via in-memory fallback and mocked log side effects; the async notification and real rate-limit paths remain untested.
key_decisions: Session 1: harden the seed — timezone-aware UTC timestamps, strict input/type validation, and init_db() at import time so the app works under a WSGI server and test runner.
Session 2: JWT bearer authentication (PyJWT) with per-user task ownership and a backward-compatible migration that assigns legacy tasks to a dedicated 'legacy' user instead of orphaned rows.
Session 3: asynchronous completion notifications via a Celery task (tasks.send_notification_email) routed to a dedicated 'notifications' queue, triggered only on pending/completed transitions.
Session 4: extract a BaseRepository/TaskRepository/UserRepository layer into repositories.py, slimming app.py into a pure controller while preserving all prior behavior and tests.
Session 5: add production cross-cutting concerns — rate limiting keyed by authenticated user (IP fallback) and validated cursor-based pagination with total/next_cursor envelope.
story_review.trajectory_description: Quality rose steadily across the story. Session 1 laid a disciplined foundation (validation, explicit error handling, testable import), and Session 2 built a meaningful security feature (JWT auth + ownership isolation) with a carefully reasoned data migration. Session 3 integrated an external messaging seam cleanly, Session 4 was a textbook behavior-preserving refactor that shrank app.py from inline SQL to a controller while growing test coverage, and Session 5 capped the arc with production-grade cross-cutting concerns and the most demanding tests. The only flat spots are that the integration (Celery) and rate-limiting paths are tested only through mocked/fallback behavior, leaving some seams unexercised — but code organization, test depth (0→9 passing tests), and API polish all improved monotonically.
story_review.summary: A textbook information-acquisition story: a clean, well-validated CRUD baseline was progressively extended with auth, async integration, a disciplined repository refactor, and production cross-cutting concerns, with quality and test depth improving in every session.
